The floor gets the row and compares. THIS IS THE FAIREST FLOOR IN THE SUITE: a hand-written store that wanted to wake anybody would need the same decision this write makes. Ours also opens and closes a change window per row. THE HASH IS ON BOTH SIDES: ours calls `keyOf` and the store's `get`, the floor calls `byId.get`. THE FLUSH IS INSIDE OUR NUMBER and closes a batch that queued nothing. NO INDEX IS BUILT on this arm, which is the baseline the indexed arm is read against. THE SAME SOURCE ROWS ARE RE-SENT EVERY PASS, so no pass can drift into being a real write.

reading.ours: updateEntity(slot, { rank }), then sortedComputedCollection.getValueForSlot(sortedComputed) —createOIMComputedCollectionSorted over an index, columns [rank asc]
reading.floor: swap the ranks, then indexOf/splice out and upperBound/splice in, on a sorted array
reading.caveat: AN ENTITY MOVES WITHIN ITS GROUP, NOTHING JOINS OR LEAVES. A frame swaps the ranks of band `m` and band `m + 64` in every one of the sixty-four groups for 4 values of `m`, so each group of 128 sees 8 movers. OURS IS THE SHIPPED ORDER: an `OIMIndex` over `group` (`createOIMIndexSetDriven`) and a `createOIMComputedCollectionSorted` over it with `columns: [{ column: 'rank', direction: 'asc' }]`, one sorted computed held per group. NOTHING IS REPORTED BY HAND: `updateEntity` hands the index the changed columns, the index writes the group's `rank` bucket column slot, and that slot is a source of the group's sorted computed. THE READ IS INSIDE THE TIMED BODY: the computed is pulled, so the sort runs at the first `getValueForSlot` of the frame and every group is walked once per frame on both sides. THE COUNT THIS PREDICTS, per group per frame: ours copies the previous order (`slice` of 128) and runs `Array.prototype.sort` over it with the columns comparator, each compare loading `entity` off two slots and reading `rank` off both; the floor does, per mover, `indexOf`, `splice` out, `upperBoundByRank` and `splice` in. [FIGURE STATED IN ADVANCE] V8's sort over 128 entries with 8 displaced is on the order of 128 compares plus a binary search per mover, against the floor's 8 scans and 16 splices. WHERE THEY ARE NOT EQUAL: ours re-sorts the whole group however few entities moved, where the floor touches only the movers, which inflates our ratio; ours sorts once for all eight movers, which flatters us; and ours additionally walks the patch, marks the entity slot and the bucket column slot on the channel per `updateEntity`, which the floor's plain field store does not.

reading.caveat: AN ADDRESS OF TWO IDENTITIES AGAINST AN ADDRESS OF TWO STRINGS. Ours walks the composite key tree `OIMSlotStoreServiceTreeDriven` keeps: one `Map.get` keyed by the deck slot, one keyed by the shelf slot, then the bucket on the node — object-keyed hashes, no string hashing. The floor makes two string-keyed `Map.get`s and an `undefined` test. The key arrays are built outside the clock, as a caller holding the two segment identities would hold the pair. Every address hits a held bucket, so `getSlotByKey` never mints; it adds the store call and the `found !== undefined` test over the floor. Sixty-four combinations, eight decks by eight shelves, cycled on both sides. It replaces `chain-address.resolve-and-hold-vs-nested-map-get`, which held per call; no reading was ever recorded under either id.

The added link forwards `patchEntity` and returns what came back, so the difference between the two numbers is one field load, one arrow-property load and one call — per write. PREDICTED OPERATION COUNT: one extra frame of three machine operations against a write that already does sixteen or more, over 1024 rows per pass. WHICH WAY THE UNMEASURED DIFFERENCE PUSHES: against the deep arm, and only that way. The forwarding link cannot make any part of the write cheaper, so a reading AT OR BELOW 1.00 IS THE INSTRUMENT AND NOT THE DESIGN [FIGURE STATED IN ADVANCE]. WHAT IS NOT PRICED HERE: the shape cost. Both arms are isolated, so each runs with ONE shape at the delegating site; a process that mixes link types pays a polymorphic site on top of what this row reads, and no row in this suite measures that yet. THE WRITE AROUND THE LINK IS IDENTICAL ON BOTH ARMS AND IS INSIDE BOTH NUMBERS: `assertNotFlushing`, `openSubframe`/`closeSubframe` on the channel, the column walk over a ONE-COLUMN patch, the equality call, the store into `slot.entity`, the report to the channel and the frame that closes the pass. ONE OPERATION IS ONE `updateEntity` OF ONE COLUMN OF ONE ROW, over a population of 1024, with a frame per pass over the population — so the frame is one part in 1024 of the row. The link is touched ONCE per operation: `updateEntity` reaches `patchEntity` and no other door. A row that removed a column would touch it twice and is not measured here.

reading.floor: three collections with the SAME forwarding class — the site sees one shape
reading.caveat: THE COST NO OTHER ROW IN THIS FILE PRICES, AND THE ONE THAT DECIDES THE SHAPE OF A LAYER API. Every other row here declares `isolate` so each arm runs with ONE shape at `OIMEntityCollection`'s `this.inner.patchEntity`; this row is what those rows deliberately keep out. Both arms write the same number of rows through the same depth over three populations round-robin, and DIFFER ONLY IN HOW MANY CLASSES stand at that one call site: three, or one constructed three times. The three classes have IDENTICAL BODIES — they are written out separately rather than generated, because a factory hands back one class and that is the other arm. WHAT IT DECIDES: whether a consumer may freely mix layer types, or whether a layer API should be one class parameterised by a callback. If this row is flat, the question is answered and nothing follows from it; if it is not, then every count in the rows above is a floor rather than the price [FIGURE STATED IN ADVANCE]. WHICH WAY THE UNMEASURED DIFFERENCE PUSHES: against the many-classes arm and only that way — three shapes at a site cannot make it faster than one. WHY THREE AND NOT FIVE: three is inside V8's polymorphic range, so the row reads what a POLYMORPHIC site costs against a monomorphic one. What a MEGAMORPHIC site costs is a different row and this suite does not have it. OPERATION COUNT, AND IT IS NOT THE GEOMETRY THE SHARED PARAGRAPH BELOW DESCRIBES: this row runs THREE populations of 1024 and not one. One operation is one `updateEntity` of one column of one row and the link is touched once per operation, as below; what differs is the round. One round writes the same rows in each of the three worlds and closes a frame in each, so a full round is 3072 updates and 3 frames, and the count a pass consumes moves in steps of 3072 rather than of 1024. BOTH ARMS RUN THAT ONE DRIVER OVER THREE WORLDS, so at an equal operation count they perform an equal number of updates and an equal number of frames: nothing about how much work a pass does differs between the arms, only which classes stand at the delegating site. What the driver it replaced did: it took the rows per world from the WHOLE remaining count and then charged that count multiplied by the three worlds, so a pass performed up to 2048 updates more than the number the reading is divided by, and each arm was inflated by its own remainder. In that stored run that is 402432 updates performed against 400514 charged on our side and 626688 against 625872 on the floor, which moves that stored ratio by less than one part in two hundred. THE OVERSHOOT WAS A FALSE COUNT, IT IS GONE, AND IT WAS NOT WHAT AILS THIS ROW.
